description: We are a team of students from the University of Toronto and University of Waterloo studying Financial Analysis and Risk Management, Math, Computer Science, and Statistics. By combining our backgrounds in quantitative modeling, software engineering, and risk assessment, we hope to turn complex data into clear, actionable insights that benefit our planet.
summary: EarthRisk helps people look beyond the apparent good news of a greener landscape. Our interactive globe brings together NASA vegetation and soil-water records to explore a possible “green mirage”: vegetation increasing while water stored in the root zone decreases. Users can search for a place, select a land cell, compare historical trends and read a plain-language explanation. An optional AI-assisted research feature brings relevant scientific and policy context together on request. Designed for farmers, communities, environmental advocates and decision-makers, EarthRisk turns complex Earth observations into a starting point for questions about land and water. Its screening categories are exploratory indicators, not probabilities of harm or proof of causation.
details:
WHAT EARTHRISK DOES

A landscape can become greener while the water stored in its soil declines. EarthRisk helps people explore this possible “green mirage” by bringing NASA vegetation and soil-water records together on an interactive globe. Users can search for a location or select a land cell, compare historical trends, read a plain-language explanation, and request additional scientific and policy context.

EarthRisk is designed for farmers, communities, environmental advocates, researchers, and decision-makers who want a more complete picture than greenness alone can provide. Its results are a starting point for investigation, not a diagnosis of a particular farm or a prediction of damage.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Aligning two NASA datasets

EarthRisk combines monthly vegetation observations from NASA MODIS MOD13A3 Version 6.1 with monthly soil-water estimates from the NASA GLDAS Noah Version 2.1 land-surface model. MODIS normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) describes vegetation greenness; GLDAS estimates water stored in the soil.

MODIS observations are quality-filtered and aggregated from approximately 1 km source pixels to the GLDAS 0.25° grid. Records are aligned by grid cell and calendar month for the 2003–2024 analysis period. To represent root-zone soil-water storage, the workflow sums the 0–10 cm, 10–40 cm, and 40–100 cm GLDAS layers. The result is expressed in kg m−2; it is not volumetric soil moisture.

2. Exploring trends together

For a selected cell and time window, EarthRisk compares annual vegetation and root-zone soil-water trends. The interface uses color to distinguish a supported opposing-trend signal, an uncertain result, no detected divergence, and locations that have not yet been analyzed or have insufficient data. A stronger signal can highlight a place where greening and declining soil water deserve further investigation. The categories are exploratory evidence, not probabilities of harm or proof that a place is safe.

The chart puts the underlying time series beside a short explanation of the result. Users can adjust the time period, search for places, and navigate the globe. Each cell represents an area approximately 0.25° wide and tall, not a field-level measurement; its physical size varies with latitude.

3. Handling seasonal gaps

Cloud, snow, and other conditions can leave gaps in optical vegetation records. For short gaps, the browser may fit a seasonal curve and show estimated segments as dashed green lines alongside observed values. The original observations are preserved. These estimates can also contribute to the displayed screening result, and their uncertainty is not propagated into the statistical tests. Longer or otherwise unsupported gaps remain missing.

4. Progressive coverage

A cloud-hosted Python worker retrieves and processes historical vegetation data and publishes completed tiles to the deployed application. Processing has prioritized the southern Canadian Prairies and then Canada. Coverage is still expanding: not every land cell has paired data, and the current map displays a limited set of completed cells. Updates reflect processing of historical records, not a live satellite feed.

5. Scientific and policy context on request

When a user selects the research button, EarthRisk can use DeepSeek and Tavily search to assemble a plain-language overview of relevant science and policy, with links to sources. Cached responses and request limits help conserve resources. The overview is machine-generated; its sources and applicability to a particular location should be checked.

WHY IT MATTERS

Vegetation greenness can be encouraging, but it cannot by itself reveal whether water stored in the root zone is increasing or decreasing. By placing both records in one accessible view, EarthRisk helps users ask better questions about changes in land and water.

A farmer might use a flagged area to guide a conversation about field measurements or irrigation. A watershed group or policymaker could use it to identify places for closer study. Researchers and educators can explore how two Earth-system variables behave over time. These are possible uses of the screening tool; local measurements, knowledge, and independent assessment remain essential before consequential decisions.

CASE STUDY: EXPLORING THE CANADIAN PRAIRIES

The Canadian Prairies are an initial priority because agriculture and water availability are important to the region. In the live application, search for a place in southern Alberta, Saskatchewan, or Manitoba, select an available land cell, and compare its vegetation and soil-water histories. The chart and screening result show what the available records indicate for that particular cell and selected period. Processing is ongoing, so availability and results vary by location.

TOOLS AND IMPLEMENTATION

The interactive interface is built with React, TypeScript, and Three.js. Python services handle data processing and the application API, while Google Earth Engine provides access to MODIS data. Screening calculations are performed in the browser for the selected cell and period. A cloud worker progressively prepares additional historical data for the live site. Optional research uses DeepSeek and Tavily.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

• Complete more land coverage while retaining clear missing-data states.

• Review source quality, spatial footprints, seasonal estimation, and statistical behavior across regions; quantify how estimated gaps affect uncertainty.

• Compare selected screening results with independent field observations and local expertise.

• Investigate whether additional satellite and surface-water datasets can improve future analysis. Higher-resolution products would require separate integration and validation; they are not part of the current screening.

EarthRisk does not establish why a trend occurred. MODIS vegetation observations and modeled GLDAS soil-water storage describe different aspects of the land system, and their spatial and temporal limitations matter when interpreting a result.
